species.name: Lightning Whelk
species.desc: A large creamy-white shell with brown lightning-bolt streaks, uniquely spiraling to the left.
species.habitat: Sandy Gulf shallows & mud flats
species.fact: Florida's official state shell — spirals left-handed!
species.tip: Look at low tide on sandbars — the pointed spire peeks above wet sand.
species.gulf: Found on every SW Florida beach.

species.name: Fighting Conch
species.desc: A solid, heavy shell with a flared lip and knobby spire. Orange-brown exterior with a glossy orange interior.
species.habitat: Shallow seagrass beds
species.fact: Uses its foot-like operculum to flip itself upright.
species.tip: Wade in shallow seagrass at low tide.
species.gulf: Very common on Marco Island's South Beach.

species.name: Horse Conch
species.desc: Massive orange-brown shell that can exceed 2 feet. The living animal is brilliant orange.
species.habitat: Shallow sandy bottoms
species.fact: Largest gastropod in North America.
species.tip: Hunt the deeper water just past the wave break.
species.gulf: Florida's state shell.

species.name: Junonia
species.desc: Creamy white with rows of neat square brown spots. Smooth, elongated and elegant.
species.habitat: Deep Gulf water 60–300 ft
species.fact: The holy grail of Sanibel shelling.
species.tip: Walk the beach at first light after a major storm.
species.gulf: So prized that local tradition says finders get their photo published.

species.name: Lion's Paw
species.desc: A bold ribbed scallop with large knobby ribs. Fresh specimens are deep red or orange.
species.habitat: Deep offshore reefs 30–200 ft
species.fact: Deep-water scallop; its red color fades in sunlight.
species.tip: Check the high tide line after northeast storms.
species.gulf: Most commonly found at Keewaydin Island and Cape Romano.

species.name: Alphabet Cone
species.desc: Cream-white with irregular orange-brown spots resembling letters. Cone-shaped.
species.habitat: Sandy Gulf bottom
species.fact: Never handle live cone snails — they can sting painfully!
species.tip: Look in the swash zone at low tide.
species.gulf: Found regularly on Marco Island beaches.

species.name: Lettered Olive
species.desc: A smooth, cylindrical shell with a glossy surface. Tan to gray with zigzag brown markings.
species.habitat: Wet sand at the surf line
species.fact: Hunts just beneath wet sand at the wave's edge.
species.tip: Look for a trail in wet sand where a live olive is.
species.gulf: One of the most common live shells.

species.name: Florida Auger
species.desc: A long, narrow, tightly wound spiral shell. Grayish-white with faint brownish spiral bands.
species.habitat: Sandy intertidal zones
species.fact: Spirals into sand like a screw to chase worms.
species.tip: Look in the wet sand along the water's edge.
species.gulf: Common on the Sanibel Causeway beaches.

species.name: True Tulip
species.desc: Elongated with a pointed spire. Gray to orange with brown spiral lines.
species.habitat: Shallow sandy & grassy bottoms
species.fact: An active predator that drills into other mollusks.
species.tip: Check low tide areas at dawn.
species.gulf: Very common across all SW Florida beaches.

species.name: Banded Tulip
species.desc: Smooth grayish shell with fine brown spiral banding. More slender than True Tulip.
species.habitat: Sandy Gulf bottom
species.fact: Smaller and more common than the True Tulip.
species.tip: Often found in pairs.
species.gulf: Extremely common on Marco Island beaches.

species.name: Angel Wing
species.desc: Pure white paired shells with elegant radiating ribs — like outstretched wings. Very fragile.
species.habitat: Mud flats & sandy mud
species.fact: Buries up to 1 foot deep in mud flats.
species.tip: Search mudflat edges at extreme low tides.
species.gulf: Often found as broken halves.

species.name: Calico Scallop
species.desc: Fan-shaped with equal ribs. Colors vary wildly — white, pink, orange, purple, brown.
species.habitat: Sandy bottom
species.fact: Has up to 35 tiny eyes along its mantle edge!
species.tip: Thousands wash ashore after winter cold fronts.
species.gulf: Mass strandings happen after strong cold fronts.

species.name: Scotch Bonnet
species.desc: Rounded with a short spire, cream with spiral rows of square brown spots.
species.habitat: Sandy bottom
species.fact: North Carolina's official state shell.
species.tip: Check the drift line after major storms.
species.gulf: Uncommon but found occasionally.

species.name: Crown Conch
species.desc: Dark gray to brown with one or more rows of hollow spines.
species.habitat: Mangrove mud flats & oyster bars
species.fact: Named for the spiky crown of spines.
species.tip: Check mangrove edges at low tide.
species.gulf: Very common in Marco Island's back bays.

species.name: Kitten's Paw
species.desc: Small, ribbed, irregular shell resembling a tiny cat's paw print.
species.habitat: Attached to hard surfaces
species.fact: Attaches to rocks and oyster reefs in clusters.
species.tip: Check jetty rocks and oyster clumps.
species.gulf: Common throughout SW Florida bays.

species.name: Pear Whelk
species.desc: A pear-shaped whelk with a wide body whorl and low spire.
species.habitat: Sandy Gulf bottom
species.fact: Egg cases wash ashore in long rubbery strings.
species.tip: Look for the spiral egg case strings nearby.
species.gulf: Found on all SW Florida beaches.

species.name: Knobbed Whelk
species.desc: Large shell with distinctive knob-like protrusions on the shoulders.
species.habitat: Sandy bottom & mud flats
species.fact: Spirals right-handed, opposite of the Lightning Whelk.
species.tip: Compare spirals with Lightning Whelk.
species.gulf: Very common on all Gulf beaches.

species.name: Sunray Venus
species.desc: Glossy clamshell with radial ribs and beautiful pink to purple rays.
species.habitat: Sandy bottom
species.fact: Named for the rays of color radiating from the hinge.
species.tip: Found in shell piles after storms.
species.gulf: One of the most beautiful and common shells.

species.name: Giant Atlantic Cockle
species.desc: Large, heavy, heart-shaped clamshell with bold ribs.
species.habitat: Sandy to muddy bottom
species.fact: Has thick, prominent radial ribs that form a heart shape.
species.tip: Heavy shells that often survive intact.
species.gulf: Regularly found on Gulf beaches.

species.name: Yellow Cockle
species.desc: Heart-shaped shell with sharp, spiny radial ribs.
species.habitat: Sandy bottom
species.fact: Has spiny ridges instead of simple ribs.
species.tip: The spiny ribs make it distinctive.
species.gulf: More common on Gulf side of barrier islands.

species.name: Egg Cockle
species.desc: Small, smooth, glossy clamshell. White to cream.
species.habitat: Sandy to muddy bottom
species.fact: Smooth surface unlike other cockles.
species.tip: Delicate and often found intact.
species.gulf: Found on all SW Florida Gulf beaches.

species.name: Cross-Barred Venus
species.desc: Small to medium clamshell with fine cross-hatching ribs.
species.habitat: Sandy to muddy bottom
species.fact: Named for the cross-pattern of ribs on the shell.
species.tip: Look in sand after storms.
species.gulf: Common on all Gulf beaches.

species.name: Calico Clam
species.desc: Glossy clamshell with mottled spots and blotches.
species.habitat: Sandy bottom
species.fact: Has spots or 'calico' pattern instead of rays.
species.tip: Similar to Sunray Venus but with spot pattern.
species.gulf: Common on Gulf shell beaches.

species.name: Sand Dollar
species.desc: Flat, round, test (skeleton). Very fragile.
species.habitat: Sandy bottom
species.fact: The five holes are for tube feet used in feeding.
species.tip: Often found broken in shell piles.
species.gulf: Very common on Gulf beaches.

species.name: Coquina
species.desc: Tiny, colorful fan-shaped shell.
species.habitat: Sandy surf zone
species.fact: One of the most colorful small shells on the beach.
species.tip: Found in massive piles at the surf line.
species.gulf: One of the most abundant shells on Gulf beaches.

species.name: Apple Murex
species.desc: Spiraled gastropod with apple-round shape.
species.habitat: Sandy to rocky bottom
species.fact: Named for the apple-like shape.
species.tip: Look for round, apple-like shape.
species.gulf: Found on Gulf beaches.

species.name: Lace Murex
species.desc: Spiraled shell with frilly, lace-like ribs.
species.habitat: Rocky reefs
species.fact: Has delicate, lace-like extensions on the shell.
species.tip: Look for the lacy texture.
species.gulf: Found on Gulf beaches.

species.name: Giant Eastern Murex
species.desc: Large spiraled shell with prominent ribs.
species.habitat: Rocky reefs
species.fact: One of the larger murex shells.
species.tip: Larger murex species.
species.gulf: Uncommon in SW Florida Gulf beaches.

species.name: Rose Murex
species.desc: Spiraled shell with rosy or reddish coloring.
species.habitat: Rocky reefs
species.fact: Named for the rosy coloring.
species.tip: Look for rosy coloring.
species.gulf: Rare on SW Florida Gulf beaches.

species.name: Florida Cone
species.desc: Cone-shaped shell with smooth surface. Tan with brown markings.
species.habitat: Sandy bottom
species.fact: Smaller version of the Crown Cone.
species.tip: Smaller than Alphabet Cone.
species.gulf: Found on Gulf beaches.

species.name: Turnip Whelk
species.desc: Compact, turnip-shaped whelk with smooth, rounded whorls. Tan to gray. Less elongated than Lightning or Pear Whelk.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, moderate depths offshore
species.fact: Unlike drilling murex shells, whelks like this one pry bivalve prey open using the edge of their own shell.
species.tip: Check storm-driven beach wrack after strong offshore winds.
species.gulf: Occasional after Gulf storms push offshore drift onto SW Florida beaches.
species.location: Offshore sand flats, Sanibel & Captiva drift

species.name: Kiener's Whelk
species.desc: Subspecies of Knobbed Whelk found in Gulf waters. Knobs may be less pronounced. Gray-brown to tan.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: A Gulf-water subspecies of the Knobbed Whelk, distinguished mainly by geography and subtler shoulder knobs.
species.tip: Compare shoulder knobs closely against a Knobbed Whelk to tell the two apart.
species.gulf: Found alongside true Knobbed Whelks on Gulf beaches.
species.location: Sandy Gulf beaches, Marco Island & Naples

species.name: Gaudy Cantharus
species.desc: Small, stout shell with strong axial ribs crossed by spiral cords creating a nodulose surface. Dark brown to orange-brown.
species.habitat: Rocky areas, coral rubble, shallow waters
species.fact: Its nodulose crisscross sculpture comes from strong ribs crossing spiral cords, giving it a beaded texture.
species.tip: Flip over loose rubble and coral fragments at low tide.
species.gulf: A common small find under rocks on SW Florida jetties.

species.name: Tinted Cantharus
species.desc: Small whelk-like shell with cancellate sculpture. Gray-brown with occasional orange tint. Common under rocks in intertidal.
species.habitat: Rocky and rubble areas, shallow waters
species.fact: Closely related to the Gaudy Cantharus and often found sharing the same rubble habitat.
species.tip: Look under rocks alongside Gaudy Cantharus.
species.gulf: Common under rocks in SW Florida's intertidal zone.

species.name: Gulf Oyster Drill
species.desc: Sturdy, rough-textured shell with spiral ridges. Gray to brown, sometimes with orange-brown bands. Interior often salmon-orange.
species.habitat: Oyster reefs, rocky areas, pilings, intertidal
species.diet: Oysters and barnacles (drills a hole through the shell)
species.fact: One of the Gulf Coast's most significant oyster predators — oyster farmers actively remove it from beds.
species.tip: Check exposed oyster reefs at low tide for shells with small round drill holes.
species.gulf: A dominant predator on SW Florida oyster reefs.
species.location: Oyster bars, Naples Bay, Estero Bay, Ten Thousand Islands

species.name: Thick-Lipped Drill
species.desc: Small drill with two prominent varices and a long siphonal canal. Gray to white. Two wing-like varices give it a distinctive profile.
species.habitat: Oyster reefs, hard substrates, shallow waters
species.fact: Its two flared, wing-like varices are thought to help wedge the shell in place as it drills into oyster prey.
species.tip: Search encrusted oyster clusters at low tide.
species.gulf: An important small-scale oyster predator on Gulf reefs.
species.location: Oyster reefs, Naples Bay & Estero Bay

species.name: Tampa Drill
species.desc: Small, sturdy drill with axial ribs and spiral threads. Gray to brown. Found throughout SW Florida on oyster beds.
species.habitat: Oyster reefs, rocky areas, shallow waters
species.fact: First described from Tampa Bay, but ranges throughout SW Florida's oyster beds.
species.tip: Look among oyster clusters alongside Gulf Oyster Drills.
species.gulf: Common but often overlooked among larger drill species.
species.location: Oyster reefs, all SW Florida bays

species.name: Pitted Murex
species.desc: Small murex with distinctly pitted or cellular surface texture. White to gray. Three varices. Found under rocks and coral rubble.
species.habitat: Rocky areas, under rubble, shallow waters
species.fact: Its pitted, cellular-looking surface is unusual among local murex, most of which show spines or ribs instead.
species.tip: Sift through coral rubble at the lowest tides.
species.gulf: A small but distinctive murex found under Gulf-side rubble.

species.name: Hexagonal Murex
species.desc: Small murex with six prominent varices creating a hexagonal cross-section. White to gray. Strong axial and spiral sculpture.
species.habitat: Rocky bottoms, rubble areas, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: Its six varices create a distinct hexagonal cross-section when viewed end-on — a quick way to tell it apart from other small murex.
species.tip: Best found in dredged or storm-tossed rubble rather than dry beach sand.
species.gulf: Less ornate than the Lace Murex but a satisfying find for its geometric shape.

species.name: Mouse Cone
species.desc: Small, mouse-gray cone with a slightly elevated spire. Gray-brown with faint darker banding. Interior white.
species.habitat: Rocky and rubble areas, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: Like all cone snails it hunts using a harpoon-like, venom-tipped radula tooth — handle any live cone snail with care.
species.tip: Check shallow rubble patches at low tide, similar habitat to Alphabet Cone.
species.gulf: Less frequently found than Alphabet or Florida Cone.
species.location: Rubble flats, Bonita Beach & Marco Island

species.name: Stearns' Cone
species.desc: Small cone with tan to brownish coloring and faint spiral lines. Low spire. Found in deeper water drift more often than in shallow beach finds.
species.habitat: Sandy and rubble bottoms, moderate depths
species.fact: More often recovered from deeper-water drift material than picked up directly on the beach.
species.tip: Check shell-hash piles after dredging or major storms rather than open sand.
species.gulf: A small, easily overlooked cone in SW Florida shell drift.

species.name: Florida Miter
species.desc: Elongated, spindle-shaped shell with axial ribs and columellar folds. Tan to orange-brown. Miters are uncommon in SW Florida.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms near coral rubble, moderate depths
species.fact: Miters use a proboscis to probe sand for burrowing worms, similar in hunting style to some cone snails.
species.tip: A genuine rare find — check rubble-rich sand after big storms.
species.gulf: Uncommon enough that finding one is considered noteworthy locally.

species.name: Atlantic Yellow Cowrie
species.desc: Small, polished, egg-shaped shell. Tan to yellow-brown with tiny darker spots. Smooth, glossy surface.
species.habitat: Under rocks, coral rubble, moderate depths
species.fact: In life the mantle folds up and completely covers the shell, which is what keeps a cowrie's surface so polished.
species.tip: A true rarity this far north in the Gulf — check under rubble at the lowest tides.
species.gulf: One of the special finds of SW Florida shelling.

species.name: Coffee Bean Trivia
species.desc: Tiny, coffee-bean-shaped shell with fine transverse ribs running across the dorsum. Brown to reddish-brown.
species.habitat: Under rocks, on colonial tunicates, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: Named for its resemblance to a coffee bean, right down to the central ridge.
species.tip: Flip small rocks and look closely — these are tiny and easy to miss.
species.gulf: A common but often overlooked micro-shell.

species.name: Four-Spotted Trivia
species.desc: Tiny shell similar to Coffee Bean Trivia but with four pinkish-brown spots on the dorsum. Fine transverse ribs.
species.habitat: Under rocks, on colonial organisms, shallow waters
species.fact: The four pinkish-brown dorsal spots are the easiest way to separate it from the plainer Coffee Bean Trivia.
species.tip: Use a magnifier — at this size the spots are easy to miss.
species.gulf: Uncommon and rarely noticed even by regular beachcombers.
species.location: Under rocks, same habitat as Coffee Bean Trivia

species.name: Brown Moon Snail
species.desc: Globular shell, dark brown to chestnut. Smooth and polished. Callus partially covers umbilicus. Darker than Shark Eye.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.diet: Clams and other bivalves (drills a neat beveled hole)
species.fact: Darker overall than its cousin the Shark Eye, and its umbilicus is partially covered by a callus rather than fully open.
species.tip: Look for its telltale drilled holes in nearby clam and cockle shells.
species.gulf: A common predatory snail on Gulf sand flats.
species.location: Sandy Gulf flats, all SW Florida beaches

species.name: White Baby Ear
species.desc: Flat, ear-shaped shell with a very depressed spire — almost flat. Pure white. Smooth with fine growth lines.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow waters
species.fact: Its spire is so depressed it's almost flat, giving the shell its distinctive "ear" silhouette.
species.tip: Look for a flat, white, ear-shaped shell in wrack lines rather than upright spirals.
species.gulf: A distinctive, easily recognized find on Gulf sand flats.
species.location: Sandy flats, Fort Myers Beach & Sanibel

species.name: Shark Eye Moon Snail Egg Collar
species.desc: A rubbery, C-shaped to circular sand collar formed from sand grains cemented with mucus — the egg case of the Shark Eye Moon Snail, not a shell at all. Flexible when wet, crumbly when dry.
species.habitat: Sandy intertidal beaches, exposed after nesting
species.diet: N/A — an egg case, not a feeding shell; the snail itself preys on clams and bivalves
species.lifespan: Collar lasts days to weeks; the snail lives 3–6 years
species.fact: It's literally thousands of moon snail eggs embedded in a sand-and-mucus ribbon that the snail shapes using its own foot as a mold.
species.tip: Look for a dark, rubbery ring or partial circle in the wet sand near the tideline, especially in warmer months.
species.gulf: One of the most frequently misidentified "mystery objects" found on SW Florida beaches.
species.location: Sandy beach flats, all SW Florida Gulf beaches

species.name: Cayenne Keyhole Limpet
species.desc: Cap-shaped shell with a distinctive oval hole at the apex (keyhole). Gray to white with fine radiating ribs.
species.habitat: Rocks, hard substrates, intertidal to shallow subtidal
species.fact: The keyhole at the apex isn't decorative — it's used to expel waste and water pumped past the gills.
species.tip: Check the undersides of loose rocks in the lower intertidal.
species.gulf: A common grazer on SW Florida's rocky jetties.
species.location: Jetty rocks, Sanibel Causeway & Naples Pier

species.name: Barbados Keyhole Limpet
species.desc: Small keyhole limpet with greenish-gray coloring and radiating white ribs. Interior is white with green margin.
species.habitat: Rocks, coral rubble, intertidal
species.fact: The green-margined interior is a quick way to distinguish it from the similar Cayenne Keyhole Limpet.
species.tip: Check rocks right at the waterline where waves splash but rarely submerge.
species.gulf: Common in the high splash zone of SW Florida jetties.

species.name: Spotted Slipper Shell
species.desc: Slipper-shaped shell with brown spots or mottling on a cream background. Internal shelf present. Often found on gastropod shells.
species.habitat: On other shells and hard substrates, shallow waters
species.fact: Slipper shells are sequential hermaphrodites — they start life as males and later become female, often stacking in a chain.
species.tip: Check the undersides of larger empty gastropod shells for hitchhikers.
species.gulf: Frequently found riding along on other shells.
species.location: Attached to whelk & conch shells, all Gulf beaches

species.name: Spiny Slipper Shell
species.desc: Slipper shell with spiny or thorny exterior projections. Grayish-brown. Interior shelf present.
species.habitat: Hard substrates, rocks, other shells, shallow waters
species.fact: The spiny, thorny texture sets it apart from the many smooth-shelled slipper species in the same genus.
species.tip: Check rough surfaces — rocks, pilings, and other shells — for its distinctive spiky texture.
species.gulf: Less common than smooth slipper shells but found in the same habitats.

species.name: American Star Shell
species.desc: Thick, solid shell with a flattened base and conical spire. Cream to tan with pearly interior visible when worn.
species.habitat: Rocky areas, coral rubble, moderate depths
species.fact: Turban shells like this one have a thick calcareous operculum, sometimes called a "cat's eye," often found separately from the shell.
species.tip: Look for the round operculum nearby even if the shell itself isn't visible.
species.gulf: A heavy, solid shell that survives wave action well.

species.name: Sculptured Top Shell
species.desc: Small, conical shell with beautifully beaded spiral cords. Tan to brownish with pearly undertones.
species.habitat: Rocky and rubble areas, moderate depths
species.fact: The beaded spiral cords and pearly undertones make this one of the more elegant micro-shells found in Gulf rubble.
species.tip: Best found in rubble drift rather than open sand.
species.gulf: An attractive, easily overlooked small find.
species.location: Rubble bottoms offshore, Naples & Marco Island

species.name: Tegula-Like Top Shell
species.desc: Small, smooth, dark-colored top shell. Olive to dark brown or black. Found under rocks at low tide.
species.habitat: Rocky intertidal, under rocks, algae-covered surfaces
species.fact: Often so encrusted with coralline algae that the shell itself is hard to spot until you look closely at rocks.
species.tip: Check under rocks at low tide alongside nerites and periwinkles.
species.gulf: A common but easily camouflaged grazer.

species.name: Milk Conch
species.desc: Large, heavy, white to cream conch with a thick flared lip. Interior is glazed white, hence "milk" conch.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, seagrass beds, shallow waters near Keys
species.fact: The glossy white interior that gives it its name is unusual among Strombus-type conchs, most of which show orange or pink.
species.tip: A true rarity in SW Florida — most local finds have drifted north from Keys waters.
species.gulf: Finding one here is an unusual event worth noting.
species.location: Occasional drift, Gulf beaches (native to the Florida Keys)

species.name: Rooster Tail Conch
species.desc: Distinctive conch with a long, curved, horn-like projection extending from the outer lip like a rooster's tail. Tan to brown.
species.habitat: Sandy and rubble bottoms, moderate depths near Keys
species.fact: The long, curved spur on the outer lip — its "rooster tail" — is unmistakable but exceptionally rare to find intact this far north.
species.tip: Check storm wrack after major tropical systems, when southern drift is more likely.
species.gulf: One of the rarest conchs to turn up on a SW Florida beach.
species.location: Rare Gulf drift, native to Keys waters

species.name: Eastern Turritella
species.desc: Very elongated, many-whorled spiral shell with prominent spiral ridges. Tan to brown. Like a stretched-out screw.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, moderate depths
species.fact: Unlike true augers, its sculpture runs in spiral ridges rather than axial ribs — a good way to tell the two "screw shells" apart.
species.tip: Check muddy sand patches at low tide alongside other turret shells.
species.gulf: A common tightly-coiled spiral in Gulf shell drift.

species.name: Boring Turret Shell
species.desc: Elongated spiral similar to Eastern Turritella but smaller and with finer sculpture. Tan to gray. Often found in shell hash.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: A smaller, finer-sculptured cousin of the Eastern Turritella, often mixed in with shell hash.
species.tip: Sift through fine shell hash rather than searching visually.
species.gulf: Common but small enough to be easily overlooked.

species.name: Worm Shell (Irregular)
species.desc: Not a typical snail — grows as irregular, tube-like whorls cemented to hard surfaces. White to tan. Often mistaken for worm tubes.
species.habitat: Attached to rocks, coral, other shells, shallow waters
species.diet: Plankton (filter feeder using a mucus net)
species.fact: It starts life as a normal coiled snail, then cements itself in place and grows into a tangled, irregular tube — abandoning the typical gastropod shape entirely.
species.tip: Look for tangled, worm-like white tubes cemented to rocks rather than a loose shell.
species.gulf: Frequently mistaken for a worm tube rather than a snail.
species.location: Rocks and coral rubble, Sanibel & Naples jetties

species.name: Scaled Worm Shell
species.desc: Irregular tube shell with scaled or ribbed texture. Tan to brown. Attached to substrate. More textured than smooth Worm Shell.
species.habitat: Rocks, coral, hard substrates, shallow waters
species.fact: Its ribbed, scaled texture makes it easy to tell apart from the smoother Worm Shell when both are cemented to the same rock.
species.tip: Check the same rubble and rock surfaces as the smooth Worm Shell.
species.gulf: A textured variation on the local worm shells.
species.location: Rocks and hard substrate, Gulf-side jetties

species.name: Giant Atlantic Pyram
species.desc: Small, white, smooth, high-spired shell with flat-sided whorls. Glossy white. Three columellar folds visible in aperture.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow waters
species.fact: Rather than grazing or hunting, it pierces its worm host with a needle-like stylet and feeds on body fluids — true parasitism in miniature.
species.tip: Sift fine shell drift with a sieve — it's easy to miss by eye alone.
species.gulf: The largest and easiest-to-spot of the local pyram shells.

species.name: Interrupted Turbonilla
species.desc: Tiny, elongated white shell with axial ribs. Very narrow and pointed. Requires magnification to appreciate detail.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow waters
species.diet: Body fluids of worms and bivalves (ectoparasite)
species.fact: One of dozens of similar turbonilla species in Gulf waters, most distinguishable only with a hand lens or microscope.
species.tip: Best found by sifting sand through a fine sieve rather than searching by eye.
species.gulf: Tiny but genuinely common in beach drift once you know to look.
species.location: Fine sand drift, all Gulf beaches

species.name: Atlantic Modulus
species.desc: Small, sturdy, top-shaped shell with a prominent peripheral tooth. Gray to brownish. Heavily beaded sculpture.
species.habitat: Seagrass beds, shallow lagoons, mudflats
species.fact: Despite being one of the most abundant snails in Gulf seagrass beds, its tiny size means most beachcombers walk right past it.
species.tip: Sift through seagrass wrack rather than open sand.
species.gulf: Extremely common but rarely noticed due to its small size.

species.name: Impressed Odostome
species.desc: Extremely tiny, white, smooth shell with impressed sutures. Ectoparasite on oysters and other bivalves.
species.habitat: On oyster reefs, parasitic on bivalves
species.diet: Body fluids of oysters and other bivalves (ectoparasite)
species.fact: One of the smallest shells in this guide — a magnifying glass is basically required to appreciate its detail.
species.tip: Check the surface of live oyster clusters rather than beach sand.
species.gulf: Common on oyster reefs but virtually invisible to the naked eye.
species.location: Oyster reefs, Naples Bay & Estero Bay

species.name: Checkered Nerite
species.desc: Small, rounded shell with black and white checkered pattern. Found on rocks in the splash zone. Gregarious — usually found in groups.
species.habitat: Rocky intertidal, seawalls, limestone shoreline
species.fact: Nerites are gregarious and are usually found clustered together in groups rather than singly.
species.tip: Check clusters on rocks right at the waterline.
species.gulf: One of the most common small rock-dwelling snails in SW Florida.
species.location: Rocky splash zone, Sanibel Causeway & Naples seawalls

species.name: Olive Nerite
species.desc: Small, rounded, olive-green to dark greenish-black shell. Smooth. Found on mangrove roots and rocks in brackish areas.
species.habitat: Brackish waters, mangrove areas, river mouths
species.fact: Highly tolerant of brackish water, making it common well up into mangrove creeks and river mouths.
species.tip: Check mangrove prop roots at low tide rather than open Gulf beaches.
species.gulf: Common in brackish backwater habitats throughout SW Florida.

species.name: Zebra Nerite
species.desc: Tiny shell with bold black and white zebra stripes. Very striking pattern for such a small shell. Multiple color forms exist.
species.habitat: Rocky intertidal, splash zone, jetties
species.fact: Color pattern varies quite a bit between individuals — no two zebra stripes are quite the same.
species.tip: Check rocks right at the waterline near other nerite species.
species.gulf: A striking tiny shell often found alongside Checkered Nerites.

species.name: Mangrove Periwinkle
species.desc: Small, pointed shell. Variable tan, gray, brown, or orange with darker streaks. Found climbing mangrove trees well above the waterline.
species.habitat: Mangrove trunks, docks, pilings, above waterline
species.diet: Algae and lichen on mangrove bark (grazer)
species.fact: Lives almost entirely out of the water, climbing mangrove trunks well above the tideline to avoid aquatic predators like crabs.
species.tip: Look up, not down — check mangrove trunks and prop roots above the waterline.
species.gulf: One of the most visible snails in SW Florida's mangrove forests.
species.location: Mangrove shorelines, Ten Thousand Islands & Rookery Bay

species.name: Beaded Periwinkle
species.desc: Tiny, thick shell with beaded spiral sculpture. Gray to whitish. Found in clusters on rocks in the highest intertidal and splash zone.
species.habitat: Rocky splash zone, above waterline on rocks and seawalls
species.fact: Extremely tolerant of drying out, often found clustered in the highest splash zone where waves rarely reach.
species.tip: Check the driest, highest rocks — well above where waves are actively breaking.
species.gulf: Common in the uppermost splash zone of SW Florida jetties.
species.location: Seawalls and rocks, Naples & Bonita Beach

species.name: Common Nutmeg
species.desc: Sturdy, oval shell with strong cancellate (cross-hatched) sculpture. Cream to tan with brown spiral bands. Named for resemblance to a nutmeg.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, moderate to deep water drift
species.fact: The strong cross-hatched sculpture and rounded shape genuinely resemble a nutmeg seed, which is exactly where the common name comes from.
species.tip: Check shell-hash piles after dredging or major storms rather than open sand.
species.gulf: Usually arrives on local beaches from deeper offshore water.

species.name: Spiny Vase Shell
species.desc: Heavy, vase-shaped shell with prominent spines on the shoulder. Brown to tan. Interior pink to orange. A deep-water species that rarely washes ashore.
species.habitat: Rocky and coral areas, moderate to deep waters
species.fact: Its heavy, spine-studded shoulder and pink-to-orange interior make it one of the most striking, and rare, finds covered in this guide.
species.tip: A genuine trophy find — check storm wrack after major Gulf storms.
species.gulf: A deep-water species that only occasionally washes ashore.
species.location: Deep rocky/coral areas, rarely on beaches

species.name: Music Volute
species.desc: Cream to tan shell with lines and dots resembling musical notation, hence the name. Oval with a short spire. Mainly a Caribbean species.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, moderate to deep waters, Caribbean drift
species.fact: The lines and dots across its surface resemble handwritten sheet music, which is exactly how it earned its name.
species.tip: Considered a legendary find locally — mainly a Caribbean species that only rarely drifts this far.
species.gulf: One of the rarest shells that could conceivably appear on a SW Florida beach.

species.name: Brown-Banded Latirus
species.desc: Sturdy, dark brown shell with knobbed axial ribs and a prominent basal ridge. Interior white. Similar to a small tulip shell but darker.
species.habitat: Rocky areas, moderate depths
species.fact: A close relative of the True and Banded Tulip shells, but smaller, darker, and more heavily sculptured.
species.tip: Check rocky rubble the same way you would for tulip shells.
species.gulf: A sturdy, dark little cousin of the local tulip shells.
species.location: Rocky bottoms, Sanibel & Marco Island offshore

species.name: West Indian Worm Shell
species.desc: Starts as a tightly coiled turritella-like shell, then uncoils into an irregular tube. Tan to brown. Often found embedded in sponges.
species.habitat: Sponges, rubble, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: It begins life as a perfectly coiled turritella-like spiral, then abandons that shape entirely and grows into a loosely uncoiled tube.
species.tip: Look for the tightly coiled juvenile tip still attached to an otherwise irregular tube.
species.gulf: Fragments are common in beach drift even when the whole animal isn't found.
species.location: Embedded in sponges, Gulf-side reefs and rubble

species.name: Bleeding Tooth (Variant)
species.desc: Pale variant of the Bleeding Tooth Nerite with lighter cream-yellow base color but still showing the distinctive blood-red staining around the toothed aperture.
species.habitat: Rocky intertidal, splash zone
species.fact: The red staining around the tooth-like aperture folds is thought to help this species blend into red algae and coralline growth on the rocks it lives on.
species.tip: Look for the telltale blood-red staining near the aperture, even on paler individuals.
species.gulf: A paler color form of the classic Bleeding Tooth Nerite.
species.location: Rocky splash zone, Naples & Sanibel jetties

species.name: Say's False Limpet
species.desc: Limpet-shaped air-breathing snail with radiating ribs and a slightly off-center apex. Gray to brown with darker ribs. Not a true limpet.
species.habitat: Rocky intertidal, seawalls, splash zone
species.fact: Despite its limpet-like shape it's actually a pulmonate (air-breathing) snail, not a true limpet at all — hence "false" limpet.
species.tip: Check seawalls and jetty rocks at low tide — one of the most reliably found species in this guide.
species.gulf: Extremely common on hard structures throughout SW Florida.
species.location: Seawalls and rocks, all SW Florida jetties

species.name: Ball Murex
species.desc: Compact, rounded murex with short, recurved spines and a long, thin siphonal canal. Tan to cream. More compact body than other murex species.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, moderate depths
species.fact: Its long, thin, recurved siphonal canal stands out sharply against its otherwise compact, rounded body — an unusual combination among murex shells.
species.tip: Check shell-hash drift rather than open sand.
species.gulf: A compact, distinctively shaped murex found in Gulf drift.

species.name: Zigzag Scallop
species.desc: Large, flat scallop with distinctive zigzag or wavy concentric color bands. Orange, brown, and cream. Fewer ribs than Calico Scallop.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, moderate depths
species.fact: Like other scallops it can swim short distances by rapidly clapping its two valves together, jetting water out to escape predators.
species.tip: Check shell-hash drift after storms for its distinctive wavy color bands.
species.gulf: A larger, more colorful cousin of the common Calico Scallop.
species.location: Sandy Gulf flats, offshore Naples & Marco Island

species.name: Sentis Scallop
species.desc: Small, colorful scallop often bright red, orange, or purple. Strong ribs with spiny scales. Attaches to hard surfaces.
species.habitat: Rocky areas, under ledges, moderate depths
species.fact: One of the most vividly colored small scallops in the Gulf, ranging from bright red to purple depending on the individual.
species.tip: Check rocky ledge habitat rather than open sand — it attaches to hard surfaces.
species.gulf: A tiny but vividly colored find for shell collectors.

species.name: Flat Tree Oyster
species.desc: Flat, irregular, dark purple-brown shell. Grows in clusters on mangrove roots. Very thin and flat. Interior is pearly.
species.habitat: Mangrove roots, pilings, rocks, intertidal
species.fact: Grows in dense clusters directly on mangrove prop roots, anchored by tough byssal threads rather than cementing like a true oyster.
species.tip: Check exposed mangrove prop roots at low tide.
species.gulf: One of the most common shells found clinging to SW Florida mangroves.
species.location: Mangrove roots, Ten Thousand Islands & Rookery Bay

species.name: Bicolor Purse Oyster
species.desc: Small, flat oyster similar to Flat Tree Oyster but with bicolored interior — purple and cream. Thin and irregular.
species.habitat: Mangrove roots, rocks, intertidal hard surfaces
species.fact: The purple-and-cream interior is the easiest way to tell it apart from the larger Flat Tree Oyster it shares mangrove habitat with.
species.tip: Check the same mangrove roots as Flat Tree Oyster, just look for smaller shells.
species.gulf: A smaller companion species to the Flat Tree Oyster.

species.name: Candy Stick Tellin
species.desc: Small, smooth, elongated tellin with pink to rose rays on a white background, like a candy stick. Delicate and attractive.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow waters
species.fact: Tellins use one long siphon like a vacuum hose to suck up organic material from the sand surface without ever fully emerging.
species.tip: Sift fine sand at the waterline for its thin, candy-striped shell.
species.gulf: A delicate, colorful little tellin common in Gulf sand.

species.name: Tampa Tellin
species.desc: Small, white, smooth tellin. Named for Tampa Bay. Fine concentric sculpture. Often found in shell drift along with other small bivalves.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow bays
species.fact: Named for Tampa Bay, but ranges throughout the Gulf coast's sand flats including SW Florida.
species.tip: Sift shell drift alongside other small tellins.
species.gulf: A plain white companion to the more colorful local tellins.

species.name: White Atlantic Semele
species.desc: Small, round, white shell with fine concentric and radial sculpture creating a delicate pattern. Interior sometimes tinged purple or orange.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: The fine crisscross of concentric and radial sculpture creates a delicate lattice pattern unique among small local bivalves.
species.tip: Check fine shell drift alongside other small white bivalves.
species.gulf: A common small clam often overlooked in shell hash.

species.name: Purplish Semele
species.desc: Round shell with purplish tinge, especially on the interior. Cream exterior with brownish rays. Fine concentric sculpture.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, moderate depths
species.fact: The purple interior tinge is its signature feature and the easiest way to separate it from the plain White Atlantic Semele.
species.tip: Check the interior color of any unidentified small oval clam — purple staining points to this species.
species.gulf: A colorful cousin of the more common White Atlantic Semele.

species.name: White Miniature Ark
species.desc: Small, white, elongated ark with fine radial ribs. Clean white when bleached. Found in crevices and under rocks.
species.habitat: Rocky areas, under rubble, crevices, shallow waters
species.fact: Anchors itself in rock crevices with tough byssal threads rather than burrowing like most clams.
species.tip: Check crevices and the undersides of rubble at low tide.
species.gulf: A clean white ark commonly found tucked into rocky crevices.

species.name: Red-Brown Ark
species.desc: Small ark with reddish-brown hairy periostracum. Fine radial and concentric ribs create a cancellate pattern. Found in protected rocky crevices.
species.habitat: Rocky areas, coral rubble, crevices
species.fact: Its hairy reddish-brown periostracum crosses with fine ribs to create a distinctive cancellate, or crosshatched, texture.
species.tip: Check protected crevices alongside White Miniature Ark.
species.gulf: A common textured ark shell in SW Florida rock crevices.
species.location: Rocky crevices, coral rubble, Gulf-side jetties

species.name: Mossy Ark
species.desc: Rectangular ark covered with a thick, hairy, dark brown periostracum that gives a 'mossy' appearance. Strongly ribbed.
species.habitat: Rocks, coral, hard substrates, shallow waters
species.fact: Its thick, hairy, dark periostracum gives it a "mossy" look that helps camouflage it against algae-covered rocks.
species.tip: Look for its rectangular, fuzzy-coated shell attached to rocks by byssal threads.
species.gulf: A sturdy, well-camouflaged ark shell on SW Florida rock.

species.name: Gray Pygmy Venus
species.desc: Small, triangular, gray to white venus clam. Concentric ridges with fine radial ribs. Common in muddy sand areas.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, shallow waters
species.fact: A small, muddy-bottom relative of the Cross-Barred Venus, sharing the same ribbed venus-clam sculpture on a much smaller scale.
species.tip: Sift muddy sand alongside other small venus clams.
species.gulf: Common in Gulf-side muddy sand habitats.
species.location: Muddy sand flats, all Gulf bays

species.name: King Venus
species.desc: Sturdy venus clam with thick concentric lamellae. Cream to tan. Similar to Cross-Barred Venus but with wider, more blade-like ridges.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: Its wide, blade-like concentric ridges are heavier and more pronounced than those of the similar Cross-Barred Venus.
species.tip: Compare ridge thickness against Cross-Barred Venus to tell the two apart.
species.gulf: A sturdy, common venus clam on Gulf sand flats.
species.location: Sandy flats, all SW Florida beaches

species.name: Lightning Venus
species.desc: Oval, smooth shell with brown lightning-bolt zigzag markings on a cream background. Smooth surface unlike the sculptured Chione venus clams.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: Unlike most local venus clams, its surface is smooth rather than ribbed, letting its brown zigzag markings stand out clearly.
species.tip: Look for smooth (not ribbed) shells with lightning-bolt zigzag markings.
species.gulf: An attractively patterned, smooth-shelled venus clam.
species.location: Sandy flats, all SW Florida beaches

species.name: Wedding Cake Venus
species.desc: Small, delicate shell with thin, blade-like concentric lamellae stacked like layers of a wedding cake. White to cream.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: Its thin, stacked, blade-like ridges resemble the tiered layers of a wedding cake — one of the most delicately sculptured shells in this guide.
species.tip: Handle carefully — the thin lamellae chip easily.
species.gulf: One of the more delicate venus clams found in SW Florida.
species.location: Sandy flats, all SW Florida beaches

species.name: Hooked Mussel
species.desc: Dark brown to black mussel with strongly curved or hooked shape. Radial ribs. Forms dense clusters on oyster reefs and pilings.
species.habitat: Oyster reefs, pilings, rocks, hard substrates, intertidal
species.fact: Forms dense clusters on oyster reefs and pilings, anchored by strong byssal threads, and is one of the most abundant mussels in Gulf estuaries.
species.tip: Check oyster reefs and dock pilings at low tide for dense mussel clusters.
species.gulf: One of the most common mussels in SW Florida's estuarine waters.
species.location: Oyster reefs & pilings, Naples Bay & Estero Bay

species.name: Tulip Mussel
species.desc: Thin, elongated mussel. Brown periostracum over a purplish-brown shell. Found partially buried in sediment, often in seagrass beds.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, embedded in seagrass root mats
species.fact: Unlike the reef-clustering Hooked Mussel, it lives partly buried in seagrass root mats rather than attached to hard surfaces.
species.tip: Check seagrass wrack after storms rather than rocky habitat.
species.gulf: A soft-sediment mussel found in SW Florida seagrass meadows.

species.name: Flat Shipworm
species.desc: Tiny white shell at the boring end of a much larger worm-like animal. The shell itself is tiny and globe-shaped. Evidence seen as tunneled driftwood.
species.habitat: Inside wood — pilings, driftwood, docks
species.diet: Wood cellulose, digested with the help of symbiotic bacteria
species.fact: The tiny shell is just the boring tool at the head of a much larger worm-like body that can tunnel over a foot into submerged wood.
species.tip: Check tunneled, honeycombed driftwood rather than looking for a loose shell.
species.gulf: Evidence of its tunneling is far more commonly found than the shell itself.
species.location: Pilings and driftwood, all Gulf-side docks

species.name: Minor Jackknife Clam
species.desc: Long, narrow, slightly curved shell resembling a straight razor or jackknife. Green to brown periostracum over white shell. Rapid burrower.
species.habitat: Sandy surf zone, shallow subtidal
species.fact: An extremely fast burrower — in the water it can dig straight down out of sight in just a few seconds.
species.tip: Check the wrack line after storms for its straight-razor-shaped shell.
species.gulf: A common find in beach drift after rough surf.

species.name: Green Jackknife Clam
species.desc: Narrow, straight, green-tinged clam. Both ends gape. Greenish periostracum. Fast burrower digs straight down in sand.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, shallow bays
species.fact: Both ends of the shell stay open even when the animal is at rest, an adaptation for its rapid vertical burrowing lifestyle.
species.tip: Look for narrow, straight, greenish shells in muddy sand drift.
species.gulf: A fast-burrowing relative of the Minor Jackknife Clam.

species.name: Broad-Ribbed Cardita
species.desc: Sturdy, small bivalve with about 15-18 strong radial ribs. White to brown, sometimes with alternating color on ribs. Thick-shelled for its size.
species.habitat: Rocky areas, under rubble, crevices, shallow waters
species.fact: Its 15–18 strong radial ribs, sometimes alternating in color, make it one of the more boldly sculptured small bivalves in this guide.
species.tip: Check under rocks alongside ark shells.
species.gulf: A sturdy, heavily ribbed little clam found under SW Florida rocks.

species.name: Three-Toothed Cardita
species.desc: Tiny, sturdy bivalve with strong ribs. White to brownish. Three cardinal teeth visible. Very small but solidly built.
species.habitat: Sandy-rubble bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: Despite its tiny size it's a solidly built little clam, with three distinct hinge teeth that give it its common name.
species.tip: Sift rubble-rich sand alongside other tiny bivalves.
species.gulf: A tiny but sturdy cardita found in Gulf shell drift.

species.name: Atlantic Abra
species.desc: Extremely small, thin, translucent white shell. Oval-shaped. Almost transparent. Found in fine shell drift.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, shallow subtidal
species.fact: Nearly transparent in life, it's one of the most delicate and easily overlooked bivalves in Gulf sand.
species.tip: Requires careful sifting of fine sediment — easy to miss without close inspection.
species.gulf: A tiny, translucent clam common in fine shell drift.

species.name: Dwarf Surf Clam
species.desc: Tiny, triangular, inflated clam. White to yellowish. Extremely abundant in shallow bays. Found by hundreds in fine shell drift.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, shallow bays and estuaries
species.fact: One of the most numerous bivalves in Gulf estuaries — population booms can leave hundreds packed into a single scoop of sand.
species.tip: Sift shallow bay sand — you'll likely find dozens at once.
species.gulf: Extremely abundant in SW Florida's estuarine waters.
species.location: Shallow bays, all SW Florida estuaries

species.name: Cross-Hatched Lucine
species.desc: Small, round, white shell with distinctive divaricate (chevron-shaped) sculpture on the surface. Unlike any other local bivalve.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.diet: Filter feeding supplemented by sulfur-oxidizing bacteria in its gills
species.fact: Like other lucines, it hosts symbiotic bacteria in its gills that convert sulfur compounds into food — a chemosynthetic partnership similar to deep-sea vent life.
species.tip: Look for the distinctive chevron-shaped crosshatched sculpture unlike any other local shell.
species.gulf: A distinctive, uniquely patterned lucine common on Gulf beaches.
species.location: Sandy flats, all SW Florida beaches

species.name: Thick Lucine
species.desc: Round, white, thick-shelled lucine with distinct concentric ridges. Heavier than Pennsylvania Lucine. White to chalky. Common in seagrass areas.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms near seagrass, shallow to moderate depths
species.diet: Filter feeding supplemented by sulfur-oxidizing bacterial symbionts
species.fact: Lucines like this one dig a mucus-lined feeding tube to the sand surface and can live for many years in the same burrow.
species.tip: Check sandy patches within seagrass beds.
species.gulf: A heavy, long-lived lucine common in Gulf seagrass habitat.

species.name: Miniature Lucine
species.desc: Very small, round, white lucine with fine concentric growth lines. Found in shell drift among other micro-shells.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow waters
species.diet: Filter feeding supplemented by bacterial symbionts
species.fact: A miniature version of the same sulfur-bacteria partnership seen in its larger lucine relatives.
species.tip: Sift fine shell drift alongside other tiny round white bivalves.
species.gulf: A small but common member of the local lucine family.

species.name: Chestnut Clam
species.desc: Small, rounded, thick shell with strong concentric ridges. Dark chestnut-brown, sometimes with lighter bands. Very solid for its small size.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, moderate depths
species.fact: Its thick, solid shell and slow growth make it comparatively long-lived for such a small clam.
species.tip: Check muddy sand patches for its dark chestnut-brown coloring.
species.gulf: An uncommon but sturdy little clam in SW Florida mud flats.

species.name: Dietz's Corbula
species.desc: Tiny, inequivalve bivalve — right valve larger than left. White to tan. Very small. Common in fine sediment samples.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, shallow bays
species.fact: One valve is noticeably larger than the other and overlaps it at the edge — an unusual asymmetry among local bivalves.
species.tip: Sift fine sediment samples for its small, unevenly sized valves.
species.gulf: A tiny but common corbula in Gulf shell drift.

species.name: Swift's Corbula
species.desc: Tiny, inequivalve bivalve similar to Dietz's Corbula. White. Right valve overlaps left. One of many small corbulas in fine shell drift.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: Nearly identical to Dietz's Corbula and best told apart by close comparison of valve shape under magnification.
species.tip: Sift fine sediment alongside Dietz's Corbula.
species.gulf: One of several similar small corbulas found in Gulf shell drift.

species.name: Three-Lined Pandora
species.desc: Flat, pearly-white shell with three faint internal ridges. Very thin and delicate. Right valve is flat; left valve is slightly convex.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, moderate depths
species.fact: Its flat, pearly-white shell is so thin it's almost translucent, with one valve notably flatter than the other.
species.tip: Handle gently — its thin shell breaks easily even when dry.
species.gulf: A delicate, pearly little clam found in SW Florida sand.

species.name: Common Spoon Shell
species.desc: Thin, white, fragile shell with an internal spoon-shaped chondrophore (internal projection for ligament attachment). Pearly interior.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: Named for the small spoon-shaped internal projection, called a chondrophore, that anchors its ligament.
species.tip: Handle carefully — like many thin white bivalves it's fragile and easily broken.
species.gulf: A delicate, pearly-interior clam found in SW Florida shell drift.

species.name: Atlantic Rangia
species.desc: Thick, heavy, triangular clam. Gray to brown with thick periostracum. Tolerates very low salinity, found in nearly fresh water estuaries.
species.habitat: Brackish estuaries, river mouths, low salinity waters
species.fact: Remarkably tolerant of low salinity, it thrives in nearly fresh water where few other bivalves can survive.
species.tip: Check brackish river mouths and low-salinity creeks rather than open Gulf beaches.
species.gulf: A hardy estuarine clam found well upriver of typical Gulf species.
species.location: Brackish river mouths, Ten Thousand Islands & Caloosahatchee estuary

species.name: Constricted Macoma
species.desc: Thin, white to yellowish oval shell with a distinctive constriction or pinch on the posterior end. Chalky white. Thin and fragile.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, shallow bays and estuaries
species.fact: The distinctive pinch or constriction near the shell's posterior end is the single easiest field mark for identifying it.
species.tip: Feel along the posterior edge for the telltale constriction.
species.gulf: A common, thin-shelled macoma in SW Florida bay sediment.

species.name: Pink Tellin
species.desc: Smooth, thin, oval shell with a beautiful pink coloration. Some specimens are vivid pink, others are pale rose. One of the most colorful tellins.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: One of the most colorful tellins on the Gulf coast, prized by collectors for its vivid pink coloring.
species.tip: Check shell drift for its glossy pink coloring — it stands out among the more common white shells.
species.gulf: A lovely, colorful find on any SW Florida beach day.
species.location: Sandy flats, all SW Florida beaches

species.name: Fuzzy Chiton
species.desc: An eight-plated mollusk, not a shell in the traditional sense. Oval body with 8 overlapping plates surrounded by a spiny girdle. Gray-green to brown. Rolls into a ball when disturbed.
species.habitat: Rocky intertidal, splash zone, limestone shoreline
species.diet: Algae and diatoms scraped from rock surfaces (grazer)
species.fact: When dislodged from a rock, it can roll into a tight ball like a pillbug to protect its soft underside.
species.tip: Check the undersides and crevices of intertidal rocks at low tide.
species.gulf: One of the more commonly found chitons on SW Florida's rocky shorelines.
species.location: Rocky intertidal, Sanibel Causeway & Naples jetties

species.name: Squamose Chiton
species.desc: Similar to Fuzzy Chiton but with larger, smoother plates and a scaly (squamose) girdle. Green to brown. Individual plates sometimes wash up on beaches.
species.habitat: Rocky intertidal, under rocks
species.fact: Its smoother, scalier girdle plates distinguish it from the bristlier Fuzzy Chiton found in the same habitat.
species.tip: Check under rocks alongside Fuzzy Chiton and compare girdle texture.
species.gulf: A common but easily overlooked chiton on SW Florida rock.
species.location: Rocky intertidal, under rocks, Gulf-side jetties

species.name: Marbled Chiton
species.desc: Eight-plated chiton with mottled or marbled green and brown coloring. Smooth, flat plates. Individual butterfly-shaped plates are sometimes found on beaches.
species.habitat: Rocky areas, under ledges, intertidal
species.fact: Individual butterfly-shaped plates often separate from the girdle after death and wash up on the beach on their own.
species.tip: Check under rocky ledges, and look for individual butterfly-shaped plates in shell drift.
species.gulf: Its mottled green-and-brown plates are a distinctive Gulf-side find.

species.name: Common Tusk Shell
species.desc: Curved, tubular, tusk-shaped shell open at both ends. White to cream. Slightly curved like a miniature elephant tusk. A different class of mollusk from gastropods and bivalves.
species.habitat: Sandy-mud bottoms, moderate depths
species.diet: Microscopic organisms such as foraminifera, captured with thread-like tentacles
species.fact: A scaphopod, not a snail or clam — it lives buried in sediment with the narrow end poking above the surface to breathe.
species.tip: Check shell-hash drift from deeper water rather than the open beach.
species.gulf: A genuinely different class of mollusk from the more familiar snails and clams in this guide.

species.name: Ivory Tusk Shell
species.desc: Smooth, glossy, ivory-white tusk shell. Gently curved tube. Very smooth surface compared to ribbed species. Small but distinctive — looks like a tiny ivory tusk.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, moderate to deep waters
species.fact: Its glassy-smooth, ivory-white surface sets it apart from the more roughly textured Common Tusk Shell.
species.tip: Check fine shell-hash drift for its small, glossy curved tube.
species.gulf: A small but elegant scaphopod found in Gulf shell drift.

species.name: Arrowhead Sand Dollar
species.desc: Sand dollar with a distinctive arrowhead-shaped posterior notch and 5 lunules. Slightly more elongated than the common Keyhole Urchin. Tan when alive, bleaches white.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, shallow waters
species.diet: Plankton and organic detritus (filter/deposit feeder via tube feet)
species.fact: The arrowhead-shaped notch at its rear and its five lunules (slots) help water and food particles move efficiently across its body as it feeds.
species.tip: Look for whole or broken tests in the swash zone after calm tides.
species.gulf: A common cousin of the classic round Sand Dollar found throughout SW Florida.

species.name: Sea Biscuit
species.desc: Thick, inflated, biscuit-shaped echinoderm, much thicker than flat sand dollars. Oval with a raised dome. 5-petaled flower pattern on top. Brown when alive.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, seagrass beds, shallow to moderate depths
species.fact: Its thick, domed body holds far more three-dimensional structure than a flat sand dollar, giving it a genuinely biscuit-like shape.
species.tip: Check seagrass-adjacent sand patches rather than open surf zones.
species.gulf: A heavier, longer-lived relative of the more common sand dollars.

species.name: Heart Urchin
species.desc: Heart-shaped, inflated echinoderm (not flat like sand dollars). Covered with fine, velvety spines when alive. Test (skeleton) is thin and fragile.
species.habitat: Sandy bottoms, buried, shallow to moderate depths
species.diet: Organic detritus (deposit feeder, lives buried in sand)
species.fact: Unlike flat sand dollars, it lives fully buried in sand and maintains a mucus-lined burrow using specialized tube feet.
species.tip: Check storm wrack — its fragile test rarely survives intact otherwise.
species.gulf: An occasional but delicate storm-drift find on SW Florida beaches.

species.name: Long-Spined Sea Urchin Test
species.desc: Rounded test (skeleton) of the long-spined urchin. Black to dark purple. Numerous small spine bases visible on surface. The living animal has very long, brittle, venomous black spines.
species.habitat: Rocky areas, reef rubble, moderate depths
species.diet: Algae (grazer, an important reef algae control species)
species.fact: A 1983 Caribbean-wide disease outbreak wiped out roughly 90% of this species' population, and reefs are still recovering from the loss of its algae-grazing role.
species.tip: Handle with care even as a test — live animals have venomous spines, so only collect bleached, spine-free tests.
species.gulf: An ecologically important reef species found as scattered tests after storms.
species.location: Rocky reef rubble, offshore Gulf reefs

species.name: Variegated Sea Urchin Test
species.desc: Rounded, slightly flattened test. Green to white. The living animal is green with short spines and often carries bits of seagrass and shell as camouflage. Tests found on beaches are usually bleached white.
species.habitat: Seagrass beds, sandy bottoms, shallow waters
species.fact: Live animals famously camouflage themselves by holding bits of shell and seagrass over their bodies with their tube feet.
species.tip: Check seagrass wrack lines for its bleached white test.
species.gulf: A common, harmless urchin test found throughout SW Florida seagrass habitat.
